b: It’s four answers to four questions. Here we go…
1. My part-time employee misses a shift every week
Is there a way to manage an hourly part-time employee who claims a sick day nearly every week?

Our workplace has two part-time paraprofessional hourly positions. They do not come with benefits, but they pay nearly double that of our other part-time positions. This role is typically occupied by young staffers working on their certification in our field; it gives them invaluable experience in our competitive industry, and they stay for a couple of years before moving up to full-time positions. When I, a manager, or other supervisory department staff are off-site, this paraprofessional basically steps in. Most people in these roles within our organization typically max out their weekly hours and end up serving as the glue that holds the department together. This is so with one of our paraprofessionals, but not true for the other, Fergus.

Fergus is great at their job. Wonderful ideas, excellent tech skills and customer service, and fantastic programs. However, almost immediately after they started, they realized they needed health insurance and more money. So they got a second job, one with better pay and benefits. I was understanding: they did good work here, and we created a schedule that accommodated their second job hours but gave us reasonable coverage. All good. Then they realized this arrangement gave them only one day off per week, and it was at that point they seemed to develop a strategic plan: to preserve their mental and physical health, they started cherry picking one shift — out of their four here each week — to call out. It seems they’ll examine our department schedule online, guesstimate when staffing is robust enough for them not to be missed, and then call out a few hours before a shift due to “not feeling well.” And I believe them. I wouldn’t feel well either if I had to work six days a week, every week. But I have literally gotten a text from Fergus an hour before their shift saying they were taking a sick day, then drove past them walking out of a coffee shop with a friend on my way to work.

When they call out, their absence puts added work and stress on me and their coworkers. Fergus always shows up for work when they’re running a program or have an important commitment or if they see in the online schedule they need to act as de facto department manager. But when they call out, other staff end up having to cover their shift at our service desk or help customers more than we would have otherwise. And sometimes other staff are out sick or I have an important meeting that day that’s not on the calendar, and without Fergus I have to scramble last-minute to find coverage.

I’ve overheard Fergus and our other paraprofessional talking about how they wish their positions could be made full-time and how that would allow them to quit other work and devote themselves fully to our organization. But this paraprofessional position has always been classified as part-time, it was clearly advertised as such when they were hired, and they lack the certification required for full-time roles. Which leaves us with Fergus, who — you can bet money each week on which of their four shifts they’re going to miss. What can I do? Challenge Fergus on whether or not they were actually sick? If they were full-time, they’d have a limit on sick leave and be required to produce a doctor’s note for anything above a certain threshold. Not true for hourly part-timers. Do I explain to them that if they expect a reference from me at the end of this position, at this point it would be very difficult for me to describe them as dependable and trustworthy? That feels like blackmail. Again, Fergus is otherwise a good employee, but it bothers me how calculated they are with their call-in arrangement, and we really do need their scheduled coverage!

Missing 25% of their scheduled time each week — like clockwork — is a pretty big deal. Why not just talk to Fergus and name what you’re seeing? For example: “I know you’re working a lot of days every week between this job and your other part-time work, and I know that must be really draining. But you’ve been missing one shift out of four every week for months now, and it’s putting a lot of stress on the rest of the team. Obviously everyone will need sick time occasionally, but we can’t be without you for 25% of your shifts. Knowing that, can I ask you to think about whether this job makes sense for you with the rest of your schedule? You do great work when you’re here, but we need reliable coverage too.”

It’s possible that conversation will resolve it one way or another. If it doesn’t, then at that point you’d want to think about whether it makes sense for you to keep Fergus on or not, or to give them a more formal warning that you need to see X specific changes in their reliability in order to keep them on. Just because you don’t have a sick leave policy that covers them doesn’t mean you can’t lay out baseline reliability expectations for the role.
2. My manager is impossible to reach when I need answers

I’ve been working at my current company for over a decade, and so has my direct supervisor. She has a big role, with a lot of people and tasks contending for her time, so I appreciate that sometimes responses are delayed, short, or not as detailed as one might wish.

However, while she is very happy to give instructions or ask questions via email, she then does not respond to follow up, even to pressing matters that need her attention or oversight. I have two enormous projects that she has not empowered me to act on without her sign-off, but then getting her attention on emails can take weeks or multiple reminders, which feels repetitive and juvenile. If she doesn’t have a system for reading messages (some of which are in direct response to her questions!), how do I get anything done?
As a note, she doesn’t read Teams messages regularly, texting her is reserved for emergencies, and getting 30 minutes on her calendar can take a lot of acrobatics. I’m at a loss!

You need to bring this problem to her! You might be thinking she’s well aware of the pattern and how it affects your projects so what’s the point in bringing it up — but it’s actually very likely that she doesn’t realize the extent of the impact on your work. You need to tell her and ask how she wants you to handle it.

For example: “I’m finding that you’re so busy that I’m not able to get answers or sign-offs from you, and so my projects are sitting without being able to move. For example, we ended up missing the deadline on X and haven’t been able to move forward on Y, and it’s tough to get time on your calendar. I hoped we could talk about how I can better handle those situations, and maybe there’s a better system I can use to keep my work moving.”

I’d also ask whether she’d be open to a standing weekly meeting with you (even a short one, like 20 minutes) so that you could save up everything for those times (tell her you’ll be proactive about canceling it if you don’t need it that week so she can reclaim the time), and also whether there’s someone else she can deputize for some of the sign-offs you need. But ultimately this is a problem that you have to put to her, because it’s not in your power to solve on your own.

3. Asking an employee to be a reference

What are your thoughts on asking a direct report — meaning that I set work, organize their performance review, approve hours — for a reference about my ability to manage? This is my first role with that management aspect, so I don’t have other options if I want to show that range.

I’d like your advice generally; I believe it’ll be that I should avoid it as they may feel pressured to provide a positive review. The reason I’m considering it is more complex — the reporting line has become sort of artificial. I could anticipate their management being transferred to the director within the next few months. I believe I act more as a mentor than a manager due to changing circumstances, and if I didn’t sign their paychecks, I’d be asking them to speak to that.

I don’t think it really changes things one way or another that the reporting line has started to feel more artificial and that you’re acting more as a mentor than a manager — since to them, you’re still their manager and the power dynamics are still there.

But I actually think it’s fine to ask if you are very thoughtful about who you ask and how you do it. First, realize they’re going to feel obligated to say yes, given the power dynamics, so you should be very sure it’s someone who would be genuinely happy to do it. (Obviously you always want to pick references who will feel that way, because you want a glowing reference, but it’s particularly important here because of the nature of the relationship.) And you should frame it as, “I wondered whether you’d feel comfortable serving as a reference and speaking to your experience working with me, particularly around my management style. I’m aware of the potential awkwardness given that I’m your manager, so please don’t feel any obligation whatsoever, and there will be absolutely no impact on our working relationship if you’d prefer not to. I’d rather you only agree if you’re genuinely comfortable.” Even with that caveat, most people are likely to feel they have to say yes — but it’s good to spell it out (and you have to mean it, of course).
4. Sending thank-you emails to colleagues during quiet holiday weeks

Did you once write a post about sending thank-you emails to colleagues during quieter times like Thanksgiving week? Or maybe there was once a lively comment section post on this? I swear I got this practice from your site, but recent searching turned up nothing to this effect.

I have practiced this for many of the last 10 years (skipping a few where I felt salty or lacking in spoons for various reasons). I typically work the days near Thanksgiving and Christmas as I don’t travel to see family and would rather save my leave for other times. These days tend to be quiet to the point of boring, particularly when I worked in office. So they are a great time to do things that are otherwise hard to make time for (writing my annual self-evaluation was always my favorite Christmas to New Year’s week activity). That makes an excellent time to write thank-you emails to colleagues. I’ve thanked executives for their collaboration and support. I’ve told respected leaders how thrilled I was to realize they know who I am. I’ve thanked colleagues for their candor and partnerships. It’s special to slow down and be vulnerable and say, “Hey, I like working with you” or “I appreciated this thing.”
Yes! I originally wrote about it during Thanksgiving week in 2014, and then ran a letter in 2017 from someone who had been doing it annually ever since. It’s a great practice.
